Why Does This Report Matter?

Ports play a critical role in international trade, regional and domestic economic activities, and the
well-being of people and societies. Today, ports are no longer simply physical infrastructure; they
have become digital systems. Port authorities, terminal operators, shipping lines, logistics providers,
and customs are increasingly linked through shared digital platforms. This improves efficiency and
transparency in ports, but it also means that a breach in one part of the ecosystem can cascade
across others. Cybersecurity in ports is therefore a collective responsibility, and the entire ecosystem
is only as strong as its weakest link.

A cybersecurity incident at a port can halt vessel movements, prevent cargo from reaching its
destination, and compromise the safety of people and the integrity of equipment, such as robot
cranes or guided vehicles. The costs of incidents

Policy

Effective cybersecurity governance needs to clarify who is accountable, which standards apply,
how compliance is enforced, and how resources are allocated to address risks across the entire
port ecosystem. However, there is currently no widely accepted, binding global framework for
port cybersecurity. While the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the International
Ship and Port Facility (ISPS) Code provide foundations, their treatment of cybersecurity remains
limited. At the national level, roughly half of countries worldwide, specifically 104 out of 194,
as measured by the International Telecommunication Union’s Global Cybersecurity Index, have
cybersecurity legislation applicable to critical infrastructure. Fewer than half of port stakeholders
report full compliance with existing frameworks in high-income countries. This situation is even less
favorable in low- and middle-income settings, with only 28 percent of port stakeholders reporting
full compliance.

Selected recommendations:

•   National or sectoral framework: Establish a technology-neutral cybersecurity framework
    applicable to critical ports that defines cybersecurity obligations, covering governance, risk
   management, and incident reporting, with enforceable compliance mechanisms.

•  Mandatory incident reporting: Governments should establish clear obligations for ports to
    report cyber incidents to national or sectoral response bodies. Without this baseline, the sector
    operates without a shared understanding of the threats it faces, and similar vulnerabilities can
   be exploited repeatedly across different operators.

Selected recommendations:

•   Inventories and vulnerability scans: Maintain live inventories of OT and IT (information technology)
    to help assess exposure and determine vulnerability to cyber threats on a regular basis. These
    also help with the implementation and consistent updating of mitigation measures.

•   Testing: Validate business continuity plans through regular drills and tabletop exercises to
   confirm that the plans work under pressure and ensure rapid recovery in real-world scenarios.

Barriers

Cyber incidents impose system-wide costs along global supply chains and ports can no longer
protect themselves in isolation. However, human, financial, and economic barriers continue to limit
progress towards resilient supply chains.

Human error remains one of the most significant risk factors — an industry study found that 92
percent of surveyed maritime crew members opened malicious phishing emails (Chubb et al. 2022).
Yet investment in training is deeply uneven: while 87.5 percent of respondents from high-income
settings indicated that their organizations provided some cybersecurity training, more than 35
percent of respondents in low- and middle-income settings reported receiving none at all. Financially,
cybersecurity is difficult to justify to leadership because it averts losses rather than generating
revenue. Tools such as Return on Security Investment (ROSI) can help frame risk in financial terms,
but uncertainty around incident costs and probability remains a persistent obstacle, compounded by
an underdeveloped insurance market.

Finally, unclear responsibilities, information gaps, and free riding weaken incentives to invest in
cyber resilience. Clear contractual responsibilities but also trust-based collaboration are essential
to improving cybersecurity across the broader port ecosystem. However, fewer than a third of the
surveyed organizations (31 percent) participate in voluntary information-sharing mechanisms,
regardless of their country’s income level.

Selected recommendations:

•   Training: Implement role-based, recurrent cybersecurity training across all staff levels, covering
   both IT and OT threat scenarios.

•   Culture: Foster a no-blame reporting culture that treats incident disclosure as a contribution to
    collective defense rather than an admission of failure.

•   Incentives: Treat cyber-resilient supply chains as a public good and reflect this in governance
   frameworks and contractual arrangements. For example, invest in cyber resilience centers
   and cross-sector capacity building to enhance coordinated detection, intelligence sharing, and
    incident response capabilities.

This report provides recommendations to bridge these gaps, securing the digital backbone of
global maritime gateways. Ultimately, robust cyber resilience will evolve from a baseline security
requirement into a decisive competitive advantage.

Introduction

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                                2


Ports as Critical Infrastructure in a Digital Era

The maritime transport sector underpins international trade, with ports and shipping networks
carrying around 80 percent of global trade by volume (UNCTAD 2025). Beyond their role as
transport gateways, ports serve as vital nodes in supply chains, connecting producers to consumers
across continents, facilitating the movement of raw materials and finished goods, and supporting
economic development in countries at all income levels. Ports are especially important for economic
activity in low-income countries and small island developing states (SIDS); according to Verschuur
et al. (2022), low-income countries are about 1.5 times, and SIDS about 2 times, more dependent
on maritime trade than the global average. Owing to this central economic function and systemic
importance, ports are increasingly recognized as critical infrastructure (CI).

Historically, port operations were largely characterized by physical processes, localized decision-
making, and a reliance on analogue systems. Over time, however, digital technologies have been
increasingly introduced across the maritime transport sector, gradually shifting many port-related
processes away from predominantly manual operations toward more interconnected digital
systems. Where implemented, this digitalization has delivered gains in efficiency, transparency,
safety, and environmental performance (World Bank 2025a). At the same time, the growing reliance
on digital systems has fundamentally altered the risk profile of ports, bringing cybersecurity to the
fore as a defining challenge for the maritime transport sector.

Port Cyber Risk: Drivers and Consequences

As ports have become more digitally enabled, cyber risk has emerged as a defining challenge for the
maritime transport sector. Cyber insecurity is widely recognized as a systemic risk, with the World
Economic Forum’s 2026 Risk Perception Survey ranking cyber risks among the most significant
global threats across economic sectors (World Economic Forum 2026). This global assessment is
mirrored within the port community: a 2026 survey conducted by the International Association of
Ports and Harbors (IAPH) found that port authorities identify cybersecurity threats as the most
important risk factor, with 61 percent of respondents classifying cyber incidents as a high risk
(IAPH 2026). In the maritime sector, these risks are particularly acute because port operations
increasingly depend on interconnected digital systems to coordinate activities and maintain the
smooth functioning of national and global supply chains (World Bank 2025a; World Bank 2025d).
These systems support real-time data exchange among public and private actors across logistics
networks that extend well beyond the physical port perimeter. As a result, cyber disruptions
affecting port information flows can propagate rapidly across supply chains, generating cascading
economic impacts comparable to—or greater than—those caused by physical damage to port
assets. In this sense, ports function not only as physical gateways but also as critical information
infrastructures,1 whose digital resilience is central to trade continuity and economic security.




1  In this report, the term “critical infrastructure” (CI) is used as an umbrella term encompassing critical infrastructure and critical
  information infrastructure (CII). CII refers to digital networks, platforms, and supporting services whose disruption could
   significantly impact national security, public safety, or essential economic functions.

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                               3



At an operational level, these systemic risks are shaped by the increasing integration of information
technology (IT) and operational technology (OT) within port environments. Modern ports operate
complex, networked systems in which IT applications—traditionally used for data management,
commercial records, and administrative processes—are closely linked to OT systems that control
physical operations such as cargo handling, crane and conveyor movements, and energy and facility
management (Lagouvardou 2018; Li et al. 2024). This convergence is significant because IT and OT
systems have distinct security requirements and risk tolerances, and failures can affect ports in
fundamentally different ways. While cyber incidents2 affecting IT systems typically disrupt data
integrity, financial transactions, or administrative operations, incidents involving OT systems
can halt cargo movement, damage physical assets, and, in severe cases, endanger human safety.
As IT and OT systems become increasingly interconnected, cyber incidents originating in digital
environments can more readily propagate into physical operations, expanding both the likelihood
and the severity of disruption (Progoulakis et al. 2022).

At the same time, many ports are adopting advanced digital architectures—often described as “Port
4.0” or “Smart Port” systems—that integrate smart solutions and Internet of Things (IoT) devices
(de la Peña Zarzuelo 2021; Li et al. 2024). While these technologies promise significant performance
gains, they also expand the threat exposure surface by increasing system complexity and the
number of interconnected assets, users, and external interfaces that must be secured.

Structural factors further exacerbate cyber risk in ports. Many port facilities continue to rely on
legacy systems that no longer receive security updates, creating persistent and well-documented
vulnerabilities (Pseftelis et al. 2021). Beyond these technical vulnerabilities, human factors remain
a critical challenge: a large share of incidents can be traced to unintentional insiders with limited
cybersecurity awareness, weak access controls, or poor cyber hygiene (Akpan et al. 2022; Vergara
Cobos and Cakir 2024).

Together, these technological, structural, and human factors contribute to a cyber risk environment
in which incidents are becoming more frequent and more diverse across the maritime transport
sector. Recent examples from the sector, illustrated in Box 1, underscore how these risks materialize
in practice. Reported incidents targeting maritime OT systems rose sharply between 2017 and
2020 (Akpan et al. 2022), and large port complexes such as Los Angeles–Long Beach now face
hundreds of millions of intrusion attempts annually (LaRocco 2024). Publicly reported data for 2023
indicate that cybercrime and hacktivism3 account for a large share of incidents affecting maritime
transport, with hacktivist activity increasingly linked to geopolitical tensions (France Cyber Maritime
and OWN 2024; Badea et al. 2025).

The economic implications of this trend are significant. Cyber incidents in ports can act as
exogenous shocks that disrupt trade flows and economic activity far beyond the affected facility.
Past and present global crises—including the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the COVID-19

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                               5



pandemic—have demonstrated the sensitivity of maritime transport networks to systemic
disruptions, with measurable contractions in seaborne trade (Idrees et al. 2025). Cyber incidents can
generate similar cascading effects, as operational disruptions in one port propagate through tightly
coupled supply chains. Economic modeling suggests that a severe cyber incident affecting major
ports could generate losses exceeding $100 billion in the Asia-Pacific region alone (Lloyd’s List 2019),
while the prolonged shutdown of a single major U.S. port could cost its regional economy billions per
month (Varley et al. 2024). Already in 2023, the average cost of a cyber incident in the maritime
transport sector reached $550,000, a threefold increase from 2022, and ransom demands averaged
$3.2 million (Kenney and Macdonald 2023).

These disruptions have direct implications for employment and livelihoods. When cyber incidents
force ports to revert to manual processes or suspend operations, throughput declines sharply and
costs increase, threatening job stability not only at the affected facility but also across shipping,
logistics, manufacturing, and distribution networks that depend on reliable port operations. At
the same time, strengthening cybersecurity capacity in ports can contribute to job creation by
supporting demand for specialized, high-skilled roles in an expanding labor market. Cybersecurity
is among the fastest-growing occupations worldwide (World Economic Forum 2026), with posted
positions increasing by around 12 percent year-on-year despite broader economic uncertainty
(World Economic Forum 2025a). In the maritime transport sector in particular, the convergence of IT
and OT systems creates demand for specialized cybersecurity expertise. These roles typically require
advanced technical skills and continuous professional development and are associated with higher-
wage employment opportunities (Akpan et al. 2022; Progoulakis et al. 2024).

Given the potential for operational disruptions in ports to reverberate across industries and borders,
cybersecurity is not a discretionary investment for ports or the countries and supply chains that
depend on them, but a core component of economic competitiveness, workforce resilience, and
trade continuity.

Cybersecurity as a Development Challenge

Cybersecurity is increasingly recognized as a determinant of long-term economic performance.
However, cybersecurity challenges are not evenly distributed across countries. Evidence from
the International Telecommunication Union’s (ITU) Global Cybersecurity Index,4 shown in

high-income countries across all dimensions of cybersecurity capacity, with particularly large

This uneven distribution of cybersecurity capacity is particularly concerning in the maritime context,
as ports in low-income countries and SIDS handle a disproportionate share of domestic economic
activity. In many cases, the countries most reliant on their ports for economic activity are also those
least equipped to defend them against cyber threats (Vergara Cobos and Cakir 2024).

In this context, cyber risk can interact with broader structural challenges faced by ports in LMICs
and small island developing states (SIDS). Differences in institutional capacity, resource availability,
and governance arrangements may shape how quickly and comprehensively cybersecurity measures
are adopted, particularly as digital exposure increases. Addressing cybersecurity in ports is therefore
not only a technical issue, but also a development challenge—one that intersects with trade
facilitation, infrastructure resilience, and economic competitiveness.

Report Purpose, Scope, and Approach

Maritime security has traditionally focused on physical threats such as piracy and safety risks.
By contrast, cybersecurity has received comparatively less systematic attention, particularly in
the port sector. This report addresses that gap by providing a comprehensive assessment of the
cybersecurity landscape in ports worldwide and by offering recommendations for integrating
cybersecurity into port digitalization and modernization efforts. It places particular emphasis on the
challenges faced by ports in low- and middle-income countries, where gaps between cyber exposure
and cyber readiness are often most pronounced. Building on recent World Bank work (World Bank
2023b; Vergara Cobos 2024; World Bank 2025a) and new empirical evidence, the report highlights
the role of institutional, technological, human and economic factors as central drivers of cyber
resilience and vulnerability.

Consistent with this focus, the report presents adaptable, system-level guidance that can be

With interconnections and interdependencies at the core of port ecosystems, effective cybersecurity
governance is becoming increasingly important. Robust governance structures play a central role in
securing stakeholder buy-in, clarifying accountability, enabling coordination, and ensuring minimum
levels of cybersecurity (Punt et al. 2023).

This chapter examines policy as a key enabler of effective cybersecurity management in ports. It
explores how international frameworks (1.1), national legislation (1.2), and local and organizational
arrangements (1.3) shape cyber resilience across complex port ecosystems. It then concludes with
recommendations to strengthen cybersecurity governance in ports (1.4).

1.1 Global Governance

There is currently no widely accepted, binding global framework for port cybersecurity. Nevertheless,
a set of international organizations and industry bodies play an important role in shaping
expectations, principles, and reference practices. Within this landscape, the International Maritime
Organization (IMO) is the most important international organization shaping global maritime
governance frameworks. As a specialized agency of the United Nations, the IMO establishes globally
accepted rules for safety, security, and environmental protection in shipping. Its International
Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code is the primary international regulatory instrument
governing port facility security. Adopted in the aftermath of the September 11 terrorist attacks and
in force since 2004, the Code establishes a standardized framework for security governance, risk
assessment, and compliance. While it was designed primarily to address physical security risks, its
limited treatment of cybersecurity is discussed in Box 3.

Beyond safety, security, and environmental protection, the IMO plays an important role in
facilitating efficiency and reducing administrative burdens in maritime transport. Fragmented
administrative processes increase the cost of trade and can act as barriers to economic activity
(UNCTAD 2023). In this context, the IMO’s Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime
Traffic (FAL Convention) provides the binding international framework for reducing administrative
burdens related to the arrival, stay, and departure of ships, as well as associated information
exchanges between ships, ports, and public authorities (IMO n.d.b). Among other things, the FAL
Convention requires IMO Member States to establish and operate Maritime Single Windows (MSW),
digital platforms enabling the electronic submission and exchange of information required for
port calls (IMO n.d.c). While these measures aim to streamline procedures and improve efficiency,
increased reliance on digital systems also introduces new cyber vulnerabilities.

In recognition of these emerging risks, the IMO issued Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Risk
Management in 2017, subsequently updated in 2021 and 2025 (IMO 2017; IMO 2025). In March
2026, the IMO approved amendments to the FAL Convention, which will require governments to
implement cybersecurity measures to protect the MSWs underpinning the electronic ship–port data
exchange. At the same time, the IMO FAL committee also approved the IMO Strategy on Maritime
Digitalization, which establishes digitalization as an overarching IMO policy. The strategy promotes
interoperability, system standardization, data-sharing and effective data governance across
organizations and jurisdictions, reinforcing the growing integration of cybersecurity considerations
into IMO‑led digitalization efforts (IMO 2026).

Alongside IMO-led instruments, other associations have developed more targeted guidance tailored
to the specific operational context of ports. In this regard, the IAPH has played a key role by
publishing the Cybersecurity Guidelines for Ports and Port Facilities (IAPH 2021), aiming to support
ports and port facilities in a manner consistent with the IMO Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Risk
Management (IMO 2025). Also in 2025, IAPH published Cyber Resilience Guidelines for Emerging
Technologies in the Maritime Supply Chain, providing a framework for mitigating cyber threats
associated with new and evolving technologies in the maritime transport industry (IAPH 2025).

In addition to port-specific guidance, cross-sector cybersecurity standards provide a common
foundation for managing cyber risk in port environments. Frameworks such as ISO/IEC 27001
and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 translate best practices into structured
governance, controls, and measurable outcomes, enabling benchmarking, vendor integration,
and compliance across jurisdictions (ISO 2022; NIST 2024a). While not port-specific or globally-
binding, these internationally recognized models are widely applicable and increasingly relevant
in practice. For example, during the interview, Port Victoria (Seychelles) highlighted the value of
aligning with ISO standards, including to meet growing expectations from the IMO to strengthen
cybersecurity investment.

Taken together, the global governance landscape for cybersecurity in ports remains fragmented and
largely non-binding. While discussions to strengthen international regulation and coordination are
ongoing at the IMO, mandatory requirements for port cybersecurity have primarily emerged through
national governance frameworks, which are examined in the following section.

1.2 National-Level Governance: Filling the Gap

1.2.1 A Fundamental Role to Play in Driving Cyber Resilience

With international frameworks for port cybersecurity still evolving, national governance has played
a central role in improving the cyber resilience of ports. National legislation and policy frameworks
are important for translating international guidance into enforceable obligations, providing legal
clarity on responsibilities and establishing minimum expectations for cybersecurity across port
authorities, operators, and other actors within the port ecosystem.

In many countries, ports are designated as critical infrastructure, placing them within the scope of
broader national cybersecurity and resilience legislation. Such frameworks help drive investment in
cybersecurity, mandate baseline risk management and reporting practices, and create incentives
for coordination among public authorities and private operators. They are often complemented by
national cybersecurity strategies, which support a coordinated, whole-of-government approach by
aligning cybersecurity priorities with broader digital and socio-economic objectives and translating
them into concrete actions and resources (ITU 2025). Together, these instruments provide the
institutional foundation for oversight, enforcement, and accountability—functions that cannot be
delivered through voluntary or industry-led instruments alone.

coordination mechanisms within ports.

1.3.2 Cybersecurity Responsibility Across Port Governance Models

Effective cybersecurity in ports depends on local governance arrangements that define
accountability, decision-making authority, and the allocation of responsibilities across the port
ecosystem. As a result, port cybersecurity governance is closely shaped by the broader governance
model under which a port operates (IAPH 2021). Different governance systems—such as public
service, tool, landlord, and fully private models—determine how ownership, operational control, and
risk management responsibilities are distributed across the port community (World Bank 2025b).

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                                   19



These structural characteristics, in turn, influence who owns and operates critical information and
operational technology (IT and OT) systems, who sets cybersecurity requirements, and determine
how complex cybersecurity governance becomes in practice (World Bank 2025a).

In public service and tool ports, where the port authority retains a high degree of operational control,
cybersecurity responsibilities can be more readily centralized. Under these models, port authorities
are often able to apply standardized controls, define common security requirements, and coordinate
incident response across port operations. By contrast, in landlord ports—where operational
systems are largely run by private terminal operators—responsibilities for cybersecurity are more
fragmented. This fragmentation increases reliance on governance instruments such as clauses in
concession agreements, minimum standards, and reporting obligations to ensure a baseline level of
cybersecurity across the port community.

In fully private port models, cybersecurity responsibility is concentrated within the private
operator. While this can enable more integrated internal governance, it also results in greater
variation in cybersecurity practices across ports and increases reliance on national regulation and
public oversight to ensure minimum protection levels. Across these different models, the locus of
cybersecurity responsibility shifts from hierarchical public control, to negotiated public–private
arrangements, or to internal corporate governance, directly reflecting ownership and governance
structures (Figure 5).

1.3.3 Management‑Level Responsibility for Cybersecurity

Once cybersecurity responsibility is allocated through port governance structures, its effective
exercise depends on clear ownership and oversight at the management level. Evidence suggests that
explicitly assigning cybersecurity responsibility to senior management is strongly associated with
higher levels of organizational resilience (Pearlson and Novaes 2022). This is reinforced by interview
findings from this analysis, which highlight that board-level buy-in has been associated with
substantial increases in both investment and ambition in cybersecurity management. In the absence
of designated leadership, cybersecurity risks often fall between organizational silos, with limited
strategic direction and unclear accountability for decision-making during incidents (ENISA 2019).

In many ports, management-level responsibility for cybersecurity is formalized through board
oversight and senior executive roles, such as Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs) or
equivalent functions. Under several national frameworks, senior management of critical entities is
explicitly responsible for ensuring that cybersecurity risks are identified, assessed, and managed
in line with organizational objectives and regulatory obligations. At this level, responsibilities
typically include setting the cybersecurity strategy and risk appetite, approving policies and
standards, allocating financial and human resources, and overseeing compliance with national or
sectoral requirements.

Management oversight is also central to preparedness and incident response. Senior executives
are often responsible for overseeing resilience planning and exercising decision-making authority
during significant cyber incidents, particularly where impacts extend to operational continuity,
safety, or the port’s role within wider supply chains. Clear escalation pathways and defined
management responsibilities are therefore essential to ensure timely and coordinated responses
when incidents occur.

Given the multiplicity of actors operating within ports, management-level responsibility frequently
extends beyond individual organizations to encompass port-wide governance arrangements.
One mechanism used in a range of port contexts is the establishment of cybersecurity steering
committees (Box 5). At the management level, such committees provide a formal structure for
strategic oversight, enabling port authorities, terminal operators, and other key stakeholders to
align cybersecurity priorities, clarify responsibilities, and coordinate policies across organizational
boundaries. While their composition and authority vary depending on the port governance model,
these arrangements help translate assigned responsibility into more coherent governance across the
port ecosystem.

1.4 Main Takeaways and Key Recommendations

Effective governance is the cornerstone of port cybersecurity. International frameworks currently
provide mostly non-binding guidance, placing the burden of implementation on national authorities.
Many countries designate ports as critical infrastructure and have national cybersecurity
regulations that focus on core elements such as governance, accountability, risk prevention and
protection, reporting and response, and resilience and continuity. However, the effectiveness
of these frameworks ultimately depends on how they are translated into local governance
arrangements within ports, where responsibilities are assigned, oversight is exercised, and
operational measures are implemented.

Recommendation 1: Strengthen alignment between global maritime frameworks and port
cybersecurity needs

International organizations should continue to advance cybersecurity within maritime governance
frameworks by progressively integrating cyber risks into existing safety and security instruments
and developing port-relevant guidance. While non-binding instruments remain important, clearer
articulation of cybersecurity expectations for ports would support greater consistency and
convergence across countries.

Recommendation 2: Establish and enforce clear national cybersecurity governance
frameworks for ports

Governments should, where appropriate, designate ports as critical infrastructure and embed
cybersecurity requirements within national legal and regulatory frameworks. National legislation
should define clear obligations for governance, risk management, incident reporting, collaboration,
and resilience, supported by enforceable compliance and oversight mechanisms to ensure a level
playing field across port operators.

Recommendation 3: Strengthen mandatory incident reporting frameworks,
especially in LMICs

Governments should accelerate the establishment and operationalization of national or sectoral
CSIRT reporting mechanisms for ports and other critical infrastructure, ensuring clear reporting
obligations and feedback loops.

Recommendation 4: Strengthen internal cybersecurity oversight within port communities

Port authorities and Port Community System Operators should establish dedicated cybersecurity
leadership — through a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) or an equivalent multi-stakeholder
steering committee — to provide clear accountability for cyber risk management across IT and
operational technology environments. These oversight bodies should be empowered to set port-wide
cybersecurity strategies, drive investment decisions, coordinate incident response, and facilitate
information sharing among port community stakeholder.

Cyber resilience encompasses how effectively a port can prevent, respond, and recover from
incidents when they do occur. Cyber resilience therefore also encompasses how effectively a port

threats, and respond and recover in a timely and coordinated manner.

This chapter builds on established frameworks developed by recognized organizations. These include
the U.S. NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (NIST 2024a), which provides a robust framework for

infrastructure. These frameworks, coupled with insights from the survey and interviews, provide a
foundation for developing an evidence-based understanding of cyber risk in ports.

2.1 Evaluating Risk: Knowing What You Are Up Against

2.1.1 How Do Incidents Occur?

Understanding how incidents enter port systems is a prerequisite for protecting them. The
overwhelming majority of port cyber incidents documented in the literature involve the exploitation
of well-known, preventable weaknesses rather than novel techniques (Meland et al. 2021; Chubb et
al. 2022; Badea et al. 2025). This has important implications: for most ports, basic and consistent
implementation of established protective controls would materially reduce exposure of information
and operational technologies (IT and OT).

Synthesizing incident data and threat analysis from various sources, the evidence consistently
points to several recurring entry points in port environments:

•   phishing and social engineering targeting staff,

•   exploitation of unpatched software vulnerabilities in IT systems,

•   insecure or unmonitored remote access connections,

•   the IT/OT interface, where administrative networks connect to operational control systems
   without adequate segmentation,

•   third-party and supply chain access, where vendors, logistics partners, or software suppliers
    introduce exposure, and

•   physical vectors, including the use of infected Universal Serial Bus (USB) devices or unauthorized
    physical access to network equipment.

Appendix 3: Further Resources to Improve Protection provides more details on these entry points
and the systems they most commonly affect.

2.1.2 Conducting Risk Assessments

To understand how these common entry points may affect a port, it is necessary to assess the
systems and processes within it. In this report, a risk assessment is taken to be the overall process
of risk identification, analysis and evaluation (ISO 31000 2018). Assets include security technologies
(for example, closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras or cargo scanners), operational technology
(such as ship-to-shore cranes), and information technology (for example, port community systems,
vessel traffic management systems, maritime or trade single windows, and other networks).
Conducting an asset inventory also helps the organization identify critical components necessary
for business continuity. When upgrading cybersecurity and developing incident response and
business continuity plans (discussed in Section 2.2) the primary focus can then be on these
critical components.

2.1.3 Extending Risk Assessments Through Vulnerability Scans

Risks should be validated through vulnerability scans. These, also sometimes called pentesting,
detect weaknesses in the system by scanning for missing updates, patches,6 or existing
misconfigurations. Vulnerability scans should be conducted at planned intervals (for example,
annually) and when significant changes to port systems occur. They should be accompanied by an
updated risk register, which is a prioritized inventory of the most significant risks to achieving the
set objectives. It is maintained to track ownership and due dates for risk mitigation actions and to
monitor any changes to risk levels. Examples of risk mitigation actions, as well as further technical
resources for the reader, are provided in Appendix 3: Further Resources to Improve Protection.

In high-income settings, almost 69 percent of respondents conduct vulnerability scans or more
specific penetration tests at least annually, and nearly a third do so every three months or more
(Figure 8). In middle-income countries, this proportion falls to approximately half of the respondents.
By contrast, half of the respondents from low-income countries conduct vulnerability scans
less than once a year or never. The absence of routine scanning and testing leaves weaknesses
unaddressed and increases the likelihood that attempted intrusions with widely available malicious
software will succeed (NIST 2022).

2.1.4 Embracing Automated Cybersecurity Solutions

Modern cybersecurity demands speed, scale, and consistency. Automated solutions help achieve
these, and help develop a continuous, proactive approach to cyber risk management. Indeed,
IAPH member ports and experts identified artificial intelligence (AI) as one of the key emerging
technologies affecting ports worldwide (IAPH 2025). For example, Security Information and Event
Management (SIEM) can help aggregate and correlate real-time information from both IT and
OT to identify patterns, and Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) can help
coordinate responses.

While integrating AI into port cybersecurity brings regulatory, legal and ethical challenges, benefits
can be significant (Lee et al. 2025). The adoption of AI and automated processes can shorten
incident length, improve consistency and speed in incident response, and help teams cope with scale.
This, in turn, reduces team fatigue and delays in responding to known security gaps. In a recent IBM
survey, organizations reduced the time to identify and contain a cybersecurity breach by an average
of 80 days compared to those that did not use AI and automation (IBM 2025).

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                             30



Yet, the adoption of automated cybersecurity systems differs significantly between ports and
income level. Over 60 percent of World Bank survey respondents from high-income countries
use automated cybersecurity solutions, while only a quarter of those from low-income countries
reported using such systems. As agentic AI lowers the barrier for actors to exploit known
vulnerabilities automatically, closing this automation gap becomes more urgent (DNV Cyber
2026). Specifically, AI can enable the scale-up of social engineering and deepfakes including video
impersonation, facilitate vulnerability discovery, and automate manipulation against IT and
connected OT systems (Vulpe et al. 2024).

Technological evolution entails risks, but it also creates significant opportunities for organizations
that actively engage with emerging technologies rather than adopting a passive stance.
Understanding the strengths and weaknesses of new tools, such as AI and big data analytics, will
become increasingly important to ensure that risk assessments are realistic and risk mitigation
strategies are effective. AI is not the only relevant emerging technology that will substantially
impact ports. The IAPH Guidelines for Emerging Technologies in the Maritime Supply Chain
(IAPH 2025) include drone and robotics, quantum computing, green energy infrastructure, 5G,
and advanced connectivity as opportunities to increase the overall safety and efficiency of port
operations. At the same time, these will also reflect on the port’s risk landscape, as they could
become critical systems or components subject to cyber incidents with significant impacts on the
ecosystem’s overall resilience.

2.2 Incident Response and Continuity Planning

2.2.1 Integrating Cybersecurity into Business Continuity Plans

Incident response planning focuses on the immediate technical and organizational actions
needed to detect, contain, and recover from a specific cybersecurity event (Nelson et al. 2025).
Business continuity planning is a core component of incident preparation. To develop a business
continuity plan (BCP), it is necessary to identify the critical business functions required for the
continued operation of an organization. The BCP defines the strategies, resources, management
responsibilities, and procedures needed to maintain these critical functions during and after
disruptions. This includes workarounds, alternative processes, and resource (re-)allocation to keep
services running. When cyberspace is excluded from continuity planning, essential functions, such as
cargo handling, customs approvals, or vessel scheduling may lack fallback procedures and recovery
paths. This could increase port downtime and cascade into operational impacts across the port
community and the wider supply chain (NIST 2023).

The World Bank survey indicates that cybersecurity is integrated into incident response and
business continuity planning of over 80 percent of the port stakeholders in high-income countries.
This percentage drops to just over 60 percent in upper-middle-income country respondents,
43 percent for respondents from lower-middle-income countries, and 25 percent for respondents
based in low-income countries (Figure 9). Insights from interviews suggest this may be because
these ports do not have business continuity plans in the first place.

2.2.2 Practicing Business Continuity Plans

To be effective, incident response and business continuity plans should be regularly practiced and
tested through tabletop exercises and drills with clearly defined recovery time and recovery point
objectives. The literature on port resilience recommends practicing switching back to manual
operations7 to ensure a port’s ability to maintain degraded operations without core IT/OT systems
for extended periods (Varley et al. 2024).

Tabletop exercises provide cost-effective opportunities to walk through incident scenarios and
identify procedural weaknesses without disrupting live operations (Varley et al. 2024). These
exercises ensure people know what actions to take when systems are compromised, including
the correct escalation paths to report incidents, when and how to activate backup systems, how
to revert to manual operations, and how this affects OT functionality. OT environments, which
include cranes, sensors, and access gates, require precise coordination between cybersecurity and
operations teams to maintain safety and security (NIST 2023). Interviewees stressed that exercises
should involve not only technical staff but also operational leaders, communications teams, and
legal counsel to ensure a coordinated organizational response. Examples of ports conducting incident

2.2.3 Operationalizing Incident Response Using Security
Operations Centers

A Security Operations Center (SOC) is a centralized team that monitors, detects, and responds
to cyber threats in real time, and it is a critical element of incident management. Without
one, organizations may struggle to identify escalation channels, delaying or preventing
effective response.

Survey findings revealed an unexpected pattern. Middle-income countries were least likely to
operate an in-house or managed SOC, while high-income and low-income countries showed the
highest rates of SOC outsourcing. Yet interviews suggest an encouraging shift, with more low- and
middle-income port operators turning to third-party SOC services as a pragmatic way to build
capability where in-house expertise is limited. Clear reporting protocols across all staff are equally
important: at one port, maintenance personnel who noticed unusual system behavior and contacted
the SOC directly prevented an incident that could have affected the entire facility.

2.2.4 Integrating Cybersecurity into Day-to-Day
Business Operations

It is possible to make cybersecurity a core requirement for new system procurement, from planning
and budgeting to specifications, deployment, and operations. This helps embed continuous, proactive
cyber risk management practices into contracts. Concession agreements in ports can mandate
minimum cybersecurity standards, for example through (World Bank 2025c):

•   information-sharing obligations,

•   periodic cybersecurity exercises,

•   alignment with international guidelines or standards,

•   requiring access controls for users,

•   monitoring of systems,

•   clear update and vulnerability patch processes, and other measures.

By embedding these expectations into procurement and contracts, port stakeholders can ensure
that new systems integrate safely with existing IT and OT, reduce unexpected costs by avoiding
expensive retrofits, and lower the risk of operational disruption. This also strengthens vendor
accountability, as vendors must provide evidence of sound software development practices and
proof that they can provide support in the event of issues. The European Commission has proposed
a new regulation package that aims to make it easier for organizations to implement cybersecurity
by design, for example, through certification and testing of available products (European
Commission 2026).

2.3 Main Takeaways and Key Recommendations

Many ports struggle to maintain a current risk picture and implement security controls into
routine operations across IT/OT. At the same time, incident readiness remains under-practiced and
insufficiently integrated with business continuity. A central challenge of cybersecurity in ports is
the transition from one-off risk-gauging efforts to continuous outcomes-focused risk management
(IMO 2025). By integrating cybersecurity responsibilities into established processes, such as risk
management, operations oversight, business continuity planning, and procurement, ports can
strengthen resilience without creating parallel institutional frameworks.

Recommendation 1: Conduct an asset inventory

Ports should identify the key systems and processes within the port by defining the perimeter
relevant to the organization and conducting a comprehensive asset inventory. Conducting an asset
inventory also helps the organization identify critical components necessary for business continuity.
This should include IT and OT assets, and document all connections, whether intended or legacy,
between the environments.

Recommendation 2: Conduct regular risk assessments

Risk assessments should be conducted at planned intervals and when significant changes to port
systems occur. In practice, this likely means conducting a comprehensive assessment annually, with
risk-based or trigger-based reassessments.

Recommendation 3: Implement practical risk mitigation measures

System protection is a core element of cybersecurity risk management. Even relatively simple
measures, such as clearly defining acceptable user behavior for online accounts or mandatory
refresh cycles for software and physical infrastructure housing IT systems, can significantly improve
a system’s overall security posture. Procurement and contracts should embed clear responsibilities
for service providers to ensure accountability and shared responsibility. At the same time, ports
should start preparing for AI-enabled threats by strengthening identity protections, training staff
to spot social engineering threats, and validating critical instructions received through alternative
channels (NIST 2024b). Appendix 3: Further Resources to Improve Protection includes additional
guidelines, standards, diagnostic tools, and basic risk mitigation measures that ports can refer to.

Recommendation 4: Develop a business continuity plan

All ports with activities considered critical to the country’s economy should develop and regularly
update their business continuity plan. Such a plan should also include cybersecurity considerations.

Recommendation 5: Regularly test the business continuity plans through exercise drills

To be effective, incident response and business continuity plans should be regularly practiced
and tested through tabletop exercises and drills with clearly defined objectives. They should
include technical staff, operational leaders, communications teams, and legal counsel to ensure a
coordinated organizational response. These exercises help teams learn and improve for the future.

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                                 37



Ports are global gateways, connecting maritime transport to other modes of transportation. As
critical links in supply chains and logistics, the efficiency of their processes is fundamental to
ensuring functioning international trade and, therefore, global prosperity. The digitalization of port
infrastructure and operations will see fundamental growth over the next few decades. As such,
cyber risks are likely to grow at a similar pace, and port stakeholders are well advised to recognize
and anticipate such risks. Ports face a triple lock of barriers: they lack the people to manage
cyber risk, the financial incentives to prioritize it, and the market structures that would reward
collective action. These barriers are mutually reinforcing, and addressing any one of them in isolation
is insufficient.

Human capacity barriers include skills mismatches and the need for effective, specialized training,
accompanied by broad awareness programs for ports workforce. Financial barriers include funding
pressures and the perceived absence of a compelling business case. These factors reduce investment
in cybersecurity controls, as such measures avert losses rather than produce measurable revenue.
Economic barriers arise when different parties do not share the same goals and problems spill over:
if one operator cuts back on cybersecurity, it can raise risks for everyone else, creating so-called
negative externalities. Some parties may be tempted to benefit from others’ investments without
contributing themselves, free-riding8 on others (Moore 2010). On top of that, information gaps make
it hard to assess risks clearly and learn from past events. This chapter examines these key barriers
to improving cybersecurity in ports and first discusses human capacity barriers (3.1), then financial
barriers (3.2), and finally economic barriers (3.3).

3.1.1 Skills Adequacy

While organizational structures provide the framework for cybersecurity, the availability of

across all income groups. World Bank survey results, illustrated in Figure 11, underscore this reality.

possessing the necessary skills — suggesting a universal sense of being under-resourced relative to

awareness training has proven to be one of the most effective defenses against cyber incidents
to date.

Organizations should implement mechanisms to assess the impact of their training and awareness
investments and demonstrate return on investment. The effectiveness of awareness programs
can be measured through behavioral indicators such as the rate at which employees report
suspicious emails or the reduction in successful phishing simulations over time. These metrics help
organizations assess and improve their training investments.

3.2 Financial Barriers

Even where ports recognize the skills gap discussed above, they frequently cannot justify
the investment — not because they are indifferent to risk, but because the financial logic of
cybersecurity works against them. Among World Bank survey respondents, funding cybersecurity
is an important barrier for more than 50 percent of ports across all income groups. The lack of a
business case is also widely recognized as a core barrier among ports. Unlike the human capacity
barriers discussed above, financial barriers concern what ports are willing to spend. This is distinct
from the market failures discussed in Section 3.3, which persist even where the financial case
becomes clear and adequate investments are present.

Security in general and cybersecurity in particular do not provide direct revenue to an organization
but help prevent revenue losses (ENISA 2012). Insights from interviews and other publications
(IAPH 2021) suggest that port leadership buy-in is important for securing sufficient and continuous
cybersecurity investment. Where leadership buy-in is absent, quantifying the cost of cyber risks
can help in demonstrating the value of cybersecurity investment. While interviews reveal varying
attitudes regarding the benefits of using loss prevention metrics, they can be useful tools for ports
to not only consider cybersecurity investment needs, but also as a decision support tool for the
prioritization of projects.

As budgetary implications remain important for the uptake of cybersecurity measures, especially
in LMICs, the economics of cyber risk will increasingly inform investment decisions. Effective
cybersecurity does not simply scale with an increase in spending. Security leaders must ensure
that investments are strategically allocated for them to translate into meaningful protection,
while remaining aligned with the organization’s financial sustainability objectives (Carfora and
Orlando 2024). To this end, officials can translate cyber risk into financial terms to secure adequate
and efficient funding. Assigning a monetary value to cybersecurity investments relative to
potential losses avoided can help quantify “risk-to-money”. Some tools are available to guide this
exercise, such as the Return on Security Investment (ROSI) concept or the Gordon-Loeb Model,9 as
explained in Box 10.

3.3 Economic Barriers

Even where ports have well-trained personnel and a clear financial case for investment, they remain
exposed to a deeper set of failures — ones that no individual port, however well-resourced, can
resolve on its own. These are not failures of awareness or ambition, but structural features of the
market: misaligned incentives, information asymmetries, and the collective action problems that
arise when information is not available or widely shared, or when the costs of a cyber incident fall on
one actor while the benefits of security are shared across many. Understanding these dynamics is
essential, because no amount of training or internal investment can fully substitute for the systemic
changes they demand.

In some cases, individual cybersecurity efforts by a single port stakeholder protect the wider
port community, thereby generating positive externalities. At the same time, when the costs of
cybersecurity are private and concentrated—borne by a single actor while benefits are shared
across the ecosystem—there is a significant risk of free‑riding (Varian 2004). Additionally, cyber
incidents at ports can propagate far beyond the affected organization, disrupting traffic, the flow
of goods, and broader supply‑chain dynamics. Where ports are designated as critical infrastructure,
the economic and societal consequences of major incidents may be so severe that governments
ultimately absorb a large share of the costs. This can create a moral hazard, as private operators
may underinvest in cybersecurity if they do not fully bear the consequences of failure (Moore 2010).
Economic theory suggests that aligning liability with the ability to prevent harm, so that those
best placed to mitigate risk also bear its costs, strengthens incentives for effective cybersecurity
investment (Anderson 2001).

Information asymmetry further undermines efficient cyber risk management. In the absence of
external mandates or incentives, operators often possess uneven or incomplete information and
may have little incentive to report incidents, particularly where disclosure could trigger liability
or reputational damage (Koepke 2017). Fragmented and incomplete information limits ports’
abilities to assess risks systematically and learn from past incidents. Similar dynamics arise in
cybersecurity markets for IT and OT systems, where vendors typically have better information
about product security than buyers. This dynamic, often referred to as a ‘Market for Lemons’10 in the
literature (Akerlof 1970), can disincentivize buyers from paying a premium for cybersecure products,

At the same time, information sharing within port ecosystems faces practical and legal constraints.
Ports and shipping companies handle commercially sensitive and legally protected information that
can complicate efforts to establish shared cybersecurity initiatives (Feport 2020). Exchanging data
on vulnerabilities, incidents, or system architectures can raise concerns related to reputational
risk, competitive disadvantage, legal liability, and compliance with data protection requirements
(Busetti and Scanni 2025; Koepke 2017). This creates structural tensions: effective cybersecurity
collaboration depends on timely and transparent information sharing, yet commercial confidentiality
and regulatory obligations may limit disclosure. Nevertheless, experience from a growing number of
formal and informal collaboration platforms suggests that, when information sharing is structured,
trusted, and governed by clearly defined rules, collective cyber resilience can be significantly
improved (ENISA 2021).

These market and coordination failures are often more pronounced in LMICs. Weaker institutional
and regulatory frameworks may fail to mandate or enforce minimum cybersecurity standards,
reducing incentives for sustained investment (Jones et al. 2021). Financial constraints and
technological gaps further limit ports’ abilities to procure cybersecurity solutions or attract skilled
professionals, increasing reliance on legacy and vulnerable systems. Information asymmetries
and underdeveloped cyber‑insurance markets compound these challenges, leaving ports not only
more exposed to cyber incidents but also less able to absorb and recover from their financial
and operational impacts. Together, these factors can lock ports into a persistent cycle of
underinvestment in cybersecurity.

3.3.2 Standardized Information-Sharing Protocols

Interview evidence suggests that the effectiveness of organization-wide collaborative arrangements

stakeholders, such as controlled file transfers, to enable operational information sharing without
increasing cyber risk. In contexts where voluntary participation remains limited, interviewees from

business partners and incentivizing engagement in collaborative cybersecurity initiatives.

3.3.3 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Beyond the Port Level

Collaboration on port cybersecurity should extend beyond the port perimeter to relevant national

information exchanged between ports, sector authorities, and global cybersecurity institutions

including data protection, liability, and mandate‑related constraints, which need to be clearly

and public authorities to participate in structured information‑sharing arrangements while

3.3.4 Aligning Economic Incentives to Improve Cyber Resilience

Systemic cyber resilience is a public good. Cybersecure ports are therefore not only in the private
economic interest of economic operators but also a core benefit to societies. This is true often
well beyond national borders, as maritime supply chains connect global markets (Verschuur et
al. 2022). When a lack of cybersecurity stems from misalignments between risks and rewards
rather than technological issues, effective solutions should focus on coordination, governance, and
realigning incentives.

Economic misalignment can be addressed by linking cybersecurity investment to incentives.
Concession agreements in ports can mandate minimum cybersecurity standards, for example,
through information-sharing obligations, periodic cybersecurity exercises, alignment with
international guidelines, or other measures (World Bank 2025c). Cost-sharing mechanisms spread
the financial burden across terminal operators, agencies, and port authorities, but must be carefully
managed to ensure wide uptake and buy-in. Examples include proportional contributions based
on throughput, shared cybersecurity funds co-financed by port authorities and operators, pooled
incident-response costs, and co-investment in port-wide cyber infrastructure. Nevertheless,
participating in shared efforts (for example, shared cyber resilience centers) should not be
considered a substitute for internal due diligence and organizational responsibility.

Clear rules on who pays when things go wrong also change behavior. Liability provisions in contracts
and insurance schemes make cyber risk explicit, so that underinvesting in cybersecurity becomes
more expensive (Kunreuther and Heal 2003). For example, contracts can state that if a company’s
failure to meet required security standards and obligations results in an incident, that company
must cover the related claims, losses, or fines. A 2019 study that modeled a global maritime
cyber event found that approximately 92 percent of the losses would not be covered by insurance
(CyRiM 2019). Clear rules can help align each organization’s self-interest with the port’s overall
resilience and discourage “free-riding”, where one company benefits from others’ investments
without contributing.

3.4 Main Takeaways and Key Recommendations

As cyber resilience is both a public and a private good, governments and private operators have an
important role to play by deploying complementary tools to improve cybersecurity. Governments
and port authorities can impose regulatory baselines, enforce compliance through audits and
sanctions, and embed cybersecurity requirements into concession agreements. On the private-
sector side, operators should recognize the interconnections within the supply chain and incorporate
cyber-risk considerations into their business engagements with purchasers, suppliers, terminal
operators, and port service providers. Businesses can leverage contractual provisions with vendors,
insurance coverage, and investment conditions tied to cyber risk considerations. When combined,
these instruments can translate systemic cyber risk into enforceable obligations and targeted
financial consequences, aligning private incentives with collective resilience objectives.

Additionally, both governments and the private sector can address the persistent deficit in
workforce capabilities across all organizational levels. Addressing these capacity deficits requires
a comprehensive approach to workforce development that spans from cultivating specialized
technical expertise among key personnel to fostering broad-based security awareness across staff
of all organizational levels (World Bank 2023a).

Strengthening port cyber resilience requires coordinated action beyond individual ports.
Information‑sharing mechanisms, cyber resilience centers, standardized protocols, and national or
international coordination platforms can reduce information asymmetries and improve collective
resilience, but only if supported by trust, clear governance, legal certainty, and appropriate
incentives. Aligning economic incentives through contractual, regulatory, and cost‑sharing
mechanisms is essential to make cybersecurity investments rational and shared economic choices.

Recommendation 1: Implement regular, role-based awareness training for all employees

Regular, role‑based awareness training helps build a security‑conscious culture by clarifying
individual responsibilities for protecting critical infrastructure (Oruc et al. 2024). Training should be
tailored to specific roles—ranging from executives and managers to IT/OT and frontline staff—and
use maritime‑specific scenarios to ensure relevance.

Recommendation 2: Invest in specialized training and professional development

Organizations should provide specialized training or professional development opportunities for
cybersecurity personnel at least annually. For low-income countries where a lack of specialized
expertise is one of the biggest barriers to becoming cyber resilient, investment in cybersecurity skills
development represents a major opportunity to enhance overall cyber resilience and build a pipeline
of high-quality jobs. Training investments should encompass the diverse roles required for maritime
transport cybersecurity, from Security Operations Center analysts and OT security engineers to
maritime risk managers and compliance specialists, also in collaboration with academic institutions.

Recommendation 3: Measure training effectiveness through behavioral metrics

Organizations should implement behavioral indicators to measure the effectiveness of awareness
programs, such as the rate at which employees report suspicious emails or the reduction in
successful phishing simulations over time. These metrics help organizations assess and improve
their training investments and demonstrate the return on investment in human capacity building.

Recommendation 4: Translate cyber risk into financial terms and build the business case for
investment

Port leadership buy‑in remains a key bottleneck, with more than 50 percent of surveyed ports
citing funding constraints and many lacking a compelling internal business case for cybersecurity
investment. To address this, ports should translate cyber risks into financial terms by linking
investments to potential losses avoided, using available frameworks and tools. Where incident cost
estimation is highly uncertain, operational metrics—such as detection and response times—can
complement financial analysis by providing concrete, decision‑relevant indicators of cybersecurity
performance. Establishing this internal business case is a necessary foundation for sustained and
prioritized cybersecurity spending.

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                              53



Recommendation 5: Align economic incentives and risk responsibilities

Governments and ports should establish clear frameworks linking cybersecurity investments to
tangible incentives. Port authorities and operators should leverage concession agreements and
liability provisions in contracts to ensure that costs, risks, and benefits are equitably distributed
across stakeholders. Information-sharing and compulsory incident reporting help to reduce
information asymmetry, facilitating coordinated risk management.

Recommendation 6: Build a layered information-sharing ecosystem, from mandatory
reporting to voluntary collaboration

Governments should accelerate the establishment of national or sectoral Computer Security Incident
Response Teams (CSIRTs) and cybersecurity frameworks for ports and other critical infrastructure,
with clear reporting obligations and feedback mechanisms—particularly in LMICs where such
systems remain underdeveloped. In parallel, ports and related actors should be encouraged to
engage in voluntary information‑sharing platforms to exchange threat intelligence and lessons
learned. For both mandatory and voluntary mechanisms to be effective, clear rules on data
ownership, confidentiality, and need‑to‑know access are essential to protect sensitive information
while enabling meaningful collaboration.
4Conclusions

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                              55



Ports sit at the center of modern economies and supply chains—and increasingly at the center of
modern cyber risk. As the sector shifts toward “Port 4.0” operations, integrates port community
systems and electronic Maritime Single Windows, and links information technologies with
operational technologies (IT with OT), cyber incidents no longer threaten only data or office systems.
They can halt vessel movements and port operations, disrupt national trade flows, create safety
risks, and propagate across the port ecosystem and beyond. In this context, cyber resilience has
become inseparable from operational resilience.

At the same time, strengthening cybersecurity does not necessarily require the creation of entirely
new institutional structures. Many of the capabilities needed to improve cyber resilience already
exist within port governance and operational practices. Ports routinely manage operational
risks, oversee third-party vendors, conduct training programs, maintain business continuity
arrangements, and coordinate among multiple stakeholders. Enhancing cybersecurity, therefore,
largely involves integrating this dimension into existing governance, risk management, capacity-
building, and operational processes. By embedding cybersecurity into established port management
functions, ports can progressively strengthen resilience while building on structures and practices
that are already familiar to operators and policymakers.

This report set out to (i) assess the global cybersecurity landscape in ports, (ii) consolidate practical
best practices, and (iii) provide strategic recommendations to improve cyber resilience in ports.
Drawing on desk-based research, global survey results, and in-depth stakeholder interviews, this
report was structured around three thematic areas that capture the key dimensions of cyber
resilience in port ecosystems, with a particular focus on low- and middle-income countries. These
themes reflect the policies and practices that consistently emerged across income contexts
as critical to the management of cyber risk, as well as key barriers to improving cybersecurity.

Limitations

The findings are subject to several limitations common to survey‑based research. First, the analysis
relies on self‑reported data, which may be subject to social desirability bias, including the potential
overstatement of cybersecurity maturity or underreporting of incidents and vulnerabilities. Second,
the number of responses limits the extent to which findings can be considered representative of the
global port sector. Third, although the survey was available in three languages, some organizations
may not have been reached equally, particularly in regions where English, French, or Spanish are
less commonly used in professional settings. Accordingly, the results should be viewed as indicative
rather than definitive, providing insights into prevailing practices and challenges rather than
statistically generalizable conclusions.

•   segmenting the network into smaller, isolated groups of devices,
•   Training users,
•   Regularly updating software,

While these twelve measures constitute basic cyber hygiene and are necessary for ensuring
cybersecurity, they may not be sufficient. The MITRE ATT&CK® database lists additional cyber
hygiene measures, such as data backups to restore systems in the event of cyber incidents, antivirus
software, and data loss prevention measures, among others. They also provide mitigation measures
relevant to operational technology (also called industrial control systems) and an overview of
detection strategies for IT, OT, and mobile.

OT-enabled systems in ports that are automated or remotely operated by third-party vendors are
widely recognized as highly vulnerable to cyber incidents, especially as IT/OT integration and remote
connectivity increase (Progoulakis et al. 2022). Cyber‑physical systems in ports tightly couple OT
with IT and human operators; remote access, shared networks, and legacy OT that is hard to patch
all expand the vulnerable surface. Recommended measures include multi-factor authentication,
time-bound access credentials, controlled access through monitored jump servers, session logging,
and clear contractual cybersecurity obligations for suppliers. Strengthening oversight of third-party
access is essential to reducing the risk of external compromise of operational systems
(Ilori et al. 2024).
